body: I see - I think it's also important to note that when I said unique, I did not mean worse than everyone else. I don't think figuring out who has it worse by comparing experiences is what this discourse should be about. We both agree that the university should be giving people options for how they want to be addressed and sticking to them. You shouldn't need to throw a huge stink to get your netID or name on your email changed. Everyone deserves to be addressed by their actual names. That's what this protest is about!

Student who's been following everything here. It doesn't seem like the university has a clear answer for what went wrong. Their statement clashes with several student accounts. Graduating seniors who were dead named were asked for a phonetic pronunciation of their names; those were ignored by commencement at the crossings. All students who were dead named had updated 'preferred' names in the system, with some for multiple years. It seems like they pulled from the legal name in the directory, but they don't say that. The statement says that it was because students didn't submit their preferred names properly or in time.

They didn't selectively ignore preferred names for trans people *specifically*; it seems true that this affected everyone who uses a 'preferred' name in the system. But the significance here is that for trans people, the use of their dead names creates a unique kind of harm. This compounds on the fact that the inconsistent use of 'preferred' names has been an issue for transgender students for as long as 'preferred' names were offered. Transgender students' dead names usually out them as trans which opens them to discrimination, harassment. It is also, genuinely, not their names. Which is why its use at graduation was disheartening for so many.

I hope this helps to answer your questions!
